question: For a set of four distinct lines in a plane, there are exactly \(N\) distinct points that lie on two or more of the lines. What is the sum of all possible values of \(N?\)
solution:
Several pairs of lines can meet at the same point, so first separate the cases in which at least three lines pass through one point.

If all four lines pass through one point, then \(N=1\).

If exactly three pass through a point \(P\), the fourth line does not pass through \(P\). It can be parallel to at most one of the three lines through \(P\). If it is parallel to one, it meets the other two, giving \(N=1+2=3\). If it is parallel to none, it meets all three, giving \(N=1+3=4\). These new intersections are distinct: two of the lines through \(P\) cannot also meet at another point.

Now suppose no three lines pass through one point. There are \(\binom{4}{2}=6\) pairs of lines. Each nonparallel pair contributes one intersection, and different pairs give distinct points because there are no triple intersections. Classifying all possible groups of parallel lines gives:

| Arrangement | Number of intersection points |
|---|---:|
| All four lines parallel | \(6-6=0\) |
| Exactly three lines parallel | \(6-3=3\) |
| Two pairs of parallel lines | \(6-2=4\) |
| Exactly one pair of parallel lines | \(6-1=5\) |
| No parallel lines | \(6\) |

Each row is possible. Use horizontal and vertical lines for the first three rows. For the fourth, use the extended sides of a trapezoid with exactly one parallel pair. For the fifth, use the three side lines of a triangle and a fourth line through no vertex and parallel to no side.

The concurrency cases and the table cover every arrangement. Counting each possible value only once, we obtain
\[
N\in\{0,1,3,4,5,6\}.
\]
Their sum is \(0+1+3+4+5+6=\boxed{19}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
